Cornelius also lists the Roman clergy: forty-six presbyters, seven deacons, seven subdeacons, forty-two acolytes, and fifty-two exorcists, readers, and doorkeepers. More than fifteen hundred widows and distressed persons are supported by the Lord's grace and kindness.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: A philosopher named Meropius of Tyre sailed to India with two boys Frumentius and Aedesius. The ship was seized and all killed except the boys who were brought to the king of Aksum. When the king died the queen asked Frumentius to help govern. Frumentius sought out Roman traders who were Christians and built churches. Later he traveled to Alexandria where Athanasius consecrated him bishop. He returned to Aksum and converted many including the king.
passage.notes: Primary Western source for the christianization of Aksum; Rufinus heard the account from Aedesius himself.

object_entity.proposition_label: Christian communities were established in the Arabian Peninsula
object_entity.description: Christianity was established in the Arabian Peninsula including at Bostra (synod c. 244), and in Himyar through Theophilus the Indian's mission c. 354 (Philostorgius); Najran attested later.

context_place.notes: Capital of the Himyarite Kingdom in South Arabia; Theophilus the Indian built a church here c. 354 per Philostorgius HE 3.4.

evidence.notes: Theophilus's Arabian mission reported by Philostorgius.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Theophilus called the Indian was sent by Emperor Constantius on an embassy to the Himyarites in south Arabia. He was originally from the island of Dibus (Socotra). He converted the Himyarites and built three churches: one in Zafar the capital, one in Aden, and one near the Persian Gulf. He also visited the Aksumites and corrected their worship.
passage.notes: Key source for Arabian/Himyarite Christianity and Theophilus's mission; preserved in Photius's epitome.
